title: A little rule (ch. 73)
hookLine: Benedict calls it a little rule for beginners

lines: A WHOLE WAY OF LIFE, WRITTEN DOWN.
cards: A man writes out a rule for a whole way of life. Prayer through the day and night, work, food, sleep, the sick, the guests, the tools, the vows, what to do when someone is late for dinner. Then he reaches the final page.

A reader might expect a flourish: this is the complete path, follow it and you'll arrive. Benedict writes something close to the opposite. He calls the whole thing a little rule, written for beginners.

teach.h: A BEGINNING, NOT A FINISH LINE.
teach.b: Chapter seventy-three opens with an admission. Benedict wrote this Rule, he says, so that by keeping it, monks might show some measure of good living and a beginning of the monastic life. A beginning, not a finish line.
For anyone hurrying on toward something more, there are better teachers.

teach.h: HE POINTS TO SCRIPTURE AND THE FATHERS.
teach.b: Then he points away from himself. First to Scripture: what page, what word of the Old and New Testaments, he asks, is not a true guide for human life?
Then to the writers before him: the holy fathers, the Conferences and Institutes of John Cassian, the lives of the desert monks, the rule of Saint Basil. Next to those, his own work is small.

And the last sentence, to whoever is reading: if you are hurrying toward your heavenly home, keep, with Christ's help, this little rule for beginners, and then, under God's protection, you will reach the greater heights he has just named.

teach.h: THESE PAST DAYS, CALLED A START.
teach.b: These past days brought hours for reading, guests received as Christ, kitchen tools treated like vessels of the altar, the sick put first, a promise to stay, the patience to bear each other.
All of that, Benedict calls a start. The humility of the ladder chapter turns out to be the author's own. And the beginner isn't someone who will soon stop being one.
In the Prologue, Benedict called his monastery a school.
Here at the end, he's still enrolling students.

how: Benedictines speak of the monastic life as a lifelong beginning, and the Rule, ending with this chapter, is read through again from the Prologue in houses that read it in a cycle.

o: a rule for novices only, set aside once they took vows
Benedict's own name for his Rule: a small guide for beginners
a pocket summary of the Rule made for busy lay readers

games.q: the closing chapter — tap the pairs.

s: Benedict ends by calling his Rule the complete path
he calls it a little rule for beginners, and points to Scripture and earlier writers for more.
chapter seventy-three points readers beyond the Rule
to the Old and New Testaments, Cassian, the lives of the desert monks and Basil's rule.
in the Rule, beginning is a stage you quickly leave behind
even at the very end, Benedict says the Rule only makes a beginning.

games.q: you've written a whole rule of life and reached the last page. how do you end it?
o: declare it the complete and perfect way.
call it a little rule for beginners, and point to greater teachers.
end with a list of punishments for those who ignore it.
games.why: Benedict calls it a little rule for beginners, and names Scripture, Cassian, the desert fathers and Basil as guides to the heights.

practice: Think of one thing from these chapters you meant to try and didn't, or tried once and dropped: the hour of reading, the guest, the patience.

Don't grade yourself; pick it up again now, the way a beginner picks up a pencil on the first day of school, and breathe out the last attempt. If you pray, borrow a psalm line from the Douay-Rheims: "Now have I begun."

wordCard.voice: A little rule. Benedict's own name for his Rule in its closing chapter: a small rule, written for beginners, pointing beyond itself to Scripture and the fathers. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: rule, the word Benedict uses for his whole book, small as he calls it.

carryVoice: Your line: always beginning. For Benedict, even the whole Rule was only a start. Until tomorrow.
